studies.title: Metformin Inhibits Hepatic mTORC1 Signaling via Dose-Dependent Mechanisms Involving AMPK and the TSC Complex
studies.finding: Pinned down HOW the diabetes drug metformin - a major longevity candidate - actually reaches mTOR. In the liver, metformin lowers cellular energy, and at low doses this shuts down mTORC1 specifically through AMPK and the TSC complex. Direct mechanistic bridge between a widely-used drug, energy sensing, and the mTOR pathway.

story: KOR2011 (2011) is a cell study showing that where lysosomes sit in the cell helps decide whether mTORC1 is on. With nutrients, lysosomes sit near the cell edge and mTORC1 is active; in starvation they cluster near the nucleus and mTORC1 output falls. Cahir O'Kane is a middle author in the author list. BER2006 (2006) is a study in cells and fruit flies showing that rapamycin, by inducing autophagy, cleared several toxic aggregate-prone proteins and reduced the toxicity of tau. Cahir O'Kane is a middle author in the author list. RAV2004 (2004) is a study in fruit flies and mice showing that inducing autophagy by blocking mTOR cleared toxic protein clumps and eased Huntington disease-like symptoms. Cahir O'Kane is a middle author in the author list.

PubMed gives no affiliation for him in these records. Related papers from the same Cambridge group list him as Cahir J O'Kane, and a 2014 paper places him in the Department of Genetics at the University of Cambridge.

studies.title: Lysosomal positioning coordinates cellular nutrient responses
studies.finding: Where the lysosome sits inside the cell helps decide whether mTORC1 is on. With nutrients available, lysosomes move to the cell periphery, physically close to the plasma-membrane signalling modules, and mTORC1 is active there; starvation changes intracellular pH and pulls lysosomes into a cluster around the nucleus, where mTORC1 output falls and autophagy is released. Lysosomal position also sets the rate of autophagosome-lysosome fusion, so one variable acts at both the initiation and the termination end of autophagic flux. This added a spatial axis to mTORC1 regulation that Rag/Ragulator recruitment alone does not account for.

studies.title: Rapamycin alleviates toxicity of different aggregate-prone proteins
studies.finding:
Building on their earlier work with mutant huntingtin, the authors showed in cell models that rapamycin, used as an autophagy inducer, increased the clearance of several proteins with long polyglutamine tracts and of a polyalanine-expanded protein, and reduced their toxicity. In fruit flies expressing wild-type or mutant human tau, rapamycin reduced tau toxicity, and this went with less insoluble tau. The authors argued that inducing autophagy with rapamycin could be useful across several aggregate-prone protein diseases, not only Huntington's disease.
Boundary: cultured cells and Drosophila overexpressing disease proteins; drawn from the abstract only; no mammalian in vivo or human data.

studies.title: Inhibition of mTOR induces autophagy and reduces toxicity of polyglutamine expansions in fly and mouse models of Huntington disease
studies.finding: Induced autophagy cleared toxic clumped proteins and improved symptoms in fly (rapamycin) and mouse (the rapalog CCI-779) models of Huntington's disease.

story: Zexing Sun was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Hematology of the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University in Hangzhou.

The single-centre review looked back at people with acquired pure red cell aplasia, a disease where the bone marrow stops making red cells. Second-line sirolimus gave a 54.5% response rate, and response did not depend on mutation status. There was no randomisation and no control arm, and the figures for ciclosporin come from different lines of treatment.

studies.title: Favorable response to second-line sirolimus regardless of STAT3/5b status in acquired pure red cell aplasia: A retrospective study from a single center.
studies.finding: Second-line sirolimus achieved a 54.5% overall response rate in ciclosporin-refractory acquired pure red cell aplasia (64.3% in secondary disease) versus 25.0% for first-line ciclosporin, with responses independent of mutation status. Observational: a single-centre retrospective series with no randomisation and no concurrent control arm. The sirolimus and ciclosporin figures come from different lines of therapy in a selected population, so confounding by indication is not excluded and the two rates should not be read as a head-to-head comparison.

studies.title: DNA methylation age analysis of rapamycin in common marmosets.
studies.finding:
The authors built two epigenetic clocks for common marmoset blood from DNA methylation data; the human-marmoset clock for relative age correlated moderately well with age in vervet monkeys and rhesus macaques. In a separate marmoset cohort they tested whether rapamycin would change epigenetic age. The clocks did not detect a significant effect of rapamycin on the epigenetic age of marmoset blood.
Boundary: a null result on one biomarker (DNA methylation age in blood). It does not show that rapamycin has no effect on aging in marmosets, only that these clocks did not register one; the abstract gives no dose, duration or group size.

story: Simone Evans is first author of a 2026 paper in eNeuro. In mouse sensory neurons without Pten, the team removed Raptor (mTORC1) or Rictor (mTORC2) to see which complex drives faster microtubule growth and larger neurons. Removing mTORC2, but not mTORC1, brought these features back to normal, and the effect was in the growth cone at the axon tip. studies.title: PTEN regulates microtubule polymerization via mTORC2, but not mTORC1, in peripheral sensory neurons
studies.finding: Uses Raptor (mTORC1) versus Rictor (mTORC2) co-deletion on a Pten-knockout background to ask which complex carries the growth signal to the microtubule cytoskeleton. Suppressing mTORC2 — but not mTORC1 — returns the accelerated microtubule polymerisation and neuronal hypertrophy of Pten-KO neurons to wild-type levels, and the effect is confined to the axonal growth cone rather than the proximal axon shaft. A clean genetic dissection on the comparatively thin mTORC2 side of the pathway.

Lysosomal position also sets the rate of autophagosome-lysosome fusion, so one variable acts at both the initiation and the termination end of autophagic flux. This added a spatial axis to mTORC1 regulation that Rag/Ragulator recruitment alone does not account for.

studies.title: Rapamycin alleviates toxicity of different aggregate-prone proteins
studies.finding:
Building on their earlier work with mutant huntingtin, the authors showed in cell models that rapamycin, used as an autophagy inducer, increased the clearance of several proteins with long polyglutamine tracts and of a polyalanine-expanded protein, and reduced their toxicity. In fruit flies expressing wild-type or mutant human tau, rapamycin reduced tau toxicity, and this went with less insoluble tau. The authors argued that inducing autophagy with rapamycin could be useful across several aggregate-prone protein diseases, not only Huntington's disease.
Boundary: cultured cells and Drosophila overexpressing disease proteins; drawn from the abstract only; no mammalian in vivo or human data.

current.lab_name: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
current.role: First author of a 2004 mouse study showing that mTOR inhibition reverses AKT-driven prostate neoplasia.
current.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Harvard Medical School (PubMed affiliation, 2004)
story: Pradip K Majumder was first author of a 2004 Nature Medicine paper in the Atlas (MAJ2004), with 12 co-authors. Mice made to express active human AKT1 in the prostate developed early prostate cancer-like growth. Treating them with an mTOR inhibitor (RAD001) killed the abnormal cells and reversed the growth. The paper also found that HIF-1 alpha targets and BCL2 could help tumours resist such treatment.

highlights.MAJ2004: First author; PubMed lists the author at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts 02115, USA.

studies.title: mTOR inhibition reverses Akt-dependent prostate intraepithelial neoplasia through regulation of apoptotic and HIF-1-dependent pathways
studies.finding: mTOR inhibition (rapamycin/RAD001) reverses Akt-driven prostate intraepithelial neoplasia in mice.

story: Nikhil Wagle was first author of the Atlas study WAG2014 in Cancer Discovery. A patient with advanced cancer had a 14-month complete response in a phase I trial of everolimus and pazopanib. Whole-exome sequencing found two MTOR mutations, and lab tests showed both switch mTOR on. This is one patient, so it gives a hypothesis and does not show a general rule for who responds. PubMed lists Wagle at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Harvard Medical School.

highlights.WAG2014: First author: found two activating MTOR mutations in a patient with an exceptional response to everolimus.

studies.finding: Two concurrent activating MTOR mutations are implicated in an extraordinary clinical response to rapalog therapy. Single-patient observation: hypothesis-generating, not evidence of a general response predictor.

current.role: First author of the 2007 phase 3 trial comparing temsirolimus, interferon alfa, or both in advanced kidney cancer.
current.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Fox Chase Cancer Center, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
story: Gary Hudes is first author of an Atlas study (HUD2007), a phase 3 randomized trial in people with poor-prognosis metastatic kidney cancer. Among 626 patients, those given temsirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, lived a median of 10.9 months, compared with 7.3 months on interferon alfa. Adding temsirolimus to interferon did not help. Rash, high blood sugar and high blood lipids were more common with temsirolimus. PubMed lists Hudes at the Fox Chase Cancer Center.

highlights.HUD2007: First author: reported the phase 3 trial in which temsirolimus alone gave longer survival than interferon alfa in poor-prognosis kidney cancer.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Medical Oncology, Fox Chase Cancer Center, Philadelphia, PA 19111, USA.

studies.title: Temsirolimus, interferon alfa, or both for advanced renal-cell carcinoma
studies.finding: Temsirolimus alone extended median overall survival to 10.9 months versus 7.3 months with interferon alfa in poor-prognosis metastatic kidney cancer; rash, hyperglycemia, and hyperlipidemia were more common with temsirolimus.

current.role: First author of the COMPETE phase 3 trial of 177Lu-edotreotide versus everolimus.
current.sub: Department of Medical Oncology, Hôpital Édouard Herriot, Lyon
story: Thomas Walter was first author of the Atlas study WALTER2026 in The Lancet, the COMPETE trial. It was an open-label phase 3 trial in 309 patients with gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, randomized 2:1. Radioligand therapy with 177Lu-edotreotide gave longer progression-free survival than everolimus (23.9 versus 14.1 months) and fewer severe treatment-related adverse events (18% versus 40%). PubMed lists Walter at the Hopital Edouard Herriot in Lyon.

highlights.WALTER2026: First author: reported the COMPETE trial result comparing 177Lu-edotreotide with everolimus.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Medical Oncology, Hôpital Édouard Herriot, Lyon, France.

studies.title: [177Lu]Lu-edotreotide versus everolimus for gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (COMPETE): a phase 3, multicentre, randomised, open-label, superiority trial.
studies.finding: Phase 3 open-label RCT (n=309, 2:1): 177Lu-edotreotide gave longer PFS than everolimus (23.9 vs 14.1 months; HR 0.67) with fewer grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events (18% vs 40%), supporting PRRT in early lines for progressive SSTR-positive GEP-NETs.
